entries.title: Back to the Future
entries.summary: Can Andy Burhnam’s vision of economic recovery in the hinterlands keep the UK together?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In Arthur Conan Doyle’s “The Story of the Lost Special” (in which Sherlock Holmes gets only a glancing reference), an entire train goes missing shortly after it has passed through Kenyon Junction. The junction was just outside the village of Culcheth in the northwest of England, where the UK’s latest prime minister, Andy Burnham, grew up. It has a claim on global history: in 1831 it became the first station where passengers could change between two independent railway lines. Here the Manchester-to-Liverpool line met the one that connected Bolton to Leigh—both created by one of the titans of the English Industrial Revolution, the engineer George Stephenson.

In Conan Doyle’s story, first published in 1898, the police inspector charged with investigating the mystery surveys the area between Kenyon Junction and the next station, at which the train has failed to arrive:

In the stretch of railway between these two points…the country is dotted with ironworks and collieries…. There are no fewer than twelve which have small-gauge lines which run trolley cars down to the main line…. Besides these, however, there are seven which have or have had proper lines running down and connecting with points to the main line, so as to convey their produce from the mouth of the mine to the great centers of distribution.

This teeming world of ironworks and collieries, by which Culcheth was closely connected to the great centers of distribution in the mother country of a global empire, is long gone. Burnham’s family moved there from Liverpool in 1971, when he was a year old. A decade earlier Kenyon Junction had closed for passenger traffic. In Burnham’s early childhood it was derelict, and during the 1970s it was completely demolished. Its station buildings, sidings, warehouses, and four platforms serving eleven lines of track evaporated as completely as Conan Doyle’s disappearing locomotive.

Lost railways (though not lost trains) featured in Burnham’s maiden speech in the House of Commons in July 2001. He introduced himself as an emissary from “the communities that were the cradle of the Industrial Revolution” and thus, in a sense, as an envoy from England’s glorious past. He had been elected as the Labour MP for Leigh, the large town nearest to his home village. “The spinning jenny,” he told Parliament, “was invented in Leigh by a poor weaver called Thomas Highs, but we were denied our place in the history books by an entrepreneur from Blackburn who quickly patented it.”

His own constituency could thus be imagined as a point of origin of the modern world. Which made it all the more poignant that, as he lamented, alongside “the closure of the mills and mines in the 1980s and 1990s,” Leigh had become “the largest town in England without a railway station.” Burnham expressed his hope that the development in Leigh of a massive new leisure and retail complex—to be called, without apparent irony, Xanadu, after the stately pleasure dome in Samuel Taylor Coleridge’s “Kubla Khan”—would allow for the rebirth of Kenyon Junction. As he explained in 2022, he had imagined naively that after that first speech “I was going to get a call from a Department for Transport civil servant the next day to say, ‘Well, and where exactly would you like this new train station, Mr. Burnham?’ It took me a while to realize that I was basically talking into the abyss.”

Burnham’s train dreams may have been interrupted by the political equivalent of Coleridge’s person from Porlock, but they were not innately fanciful. He was speaking out of an awareness that, in some profound respects, the place where he grew up, and hundreds of places like it in the North of England, had gone backwards in time. In the twenty-first century they are more disconnected from the centers of power and the leading edges of technology than they had been in the 1830s. If the old rail lines were the arteries linking northern towns to the beating heart of the empire, their severance signified a return to preindustrial peripherality.

Once, British history was centripetal—the ubiquity of industrial society pulled most of the island (and part of the neighboring island of Ireland) into the same economic and social system. But in Burnham’s lifetime it became centrifugal, creating ever wider distances between the northern and western regions and the rich heartlands of London and the southeast. Britain’s regional inequalities—in pay, disposable income, productivity, education, health, and life expectancy—are among the most severe in the developed world. In spite of the lip service to what Boris Johnson as prime minister called “leveling up,” these disparities have been largely unaltered since Burnham made his Westminster debut a quarter of a century ago.

A centrifugal economy creates a centrifugal politics. The big story of the UK this century is disjunction. In three of its four nations—Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland—the devolved governments are led by nationalists who want to disconnect from the grid of Britishness and establish independent states or, in the case of Northern Ireland, join with the rest of Ireland. The other (and overwhelmingly dominant) nation, England, voted for a different act of separation, cutting itself off from the European Union. But Brexit was also a defiance of the metropolitan center, a mutiny by the North against the Southeast. In Burnham’s Leigh, nearly two thirds of voters backed Brexit in the 2016 referendum—very much against his advice. In Makerfield, the nearby constituency he now represents, the vote was similar. This revolt was against Westminster more than Brussels.

Advertisement

Burnham’s political career has been shaped by two dark stories that between them encapsulate the sense of alienation in northwest England. One is Boys from the Blackstuff, a brilliant five-part TV drama written by Alan Bleasdale, shot on location in Liverpool and broadcast by the BBC in 1982. It followed the lives of five men who had lost their jobs in the great wave of deindustrialization set in motion by Margaret Thatcher’s rise to power in 1979. It acted out, in what felt like real time, the unraveling of British male working-class identity.

In Head North: A Rallying Cry for a More Equal Britain (2024), the manifesto he cowrote with the mayor of Liverpool, Steve Rotheram, Burnham identified a rebroadcast of the series as the spur to his decision to join the Labour Party when he was fifteen. It seems significant that the episode that had the biggest impact on him is the most unashamedly nostalgic. In “George’s Last Ride,” an old docker near death is pushed in his wheelchair along Liverpool’s once glorious Albert Dock, now largely derelict. Amid the starkly beautiful ruins, George utters his dying words:

Forty-seven years ago, I stood here, a young bull, and watched my first ship come in. They say that memories live longer than dreams. But my dreams, those dreams of long ago, they still give me hope and faith in my class…. I can’t believe that there’s no hope, I can’t.

In Head North, Burnham writes:

I remember turning away from the screen to see the tears streaming down my mum’s face. Her dad, Jimmy, had worked on those docks as a lorry driver for Tate & Lyle, as had our Irish ancestors before him. It was painfully close to home.

Even more painful was the Hillsborough disaster of 1989. Almost a hundred fans of Liverpool Football Club were crushed in a soccer stadium in Sheffield. The calamity was caused by egregious failures by the police officers in charge of crowd safety. But the fans themselves were blamed for their own deaths and mercilessly slandered as hooligans in Rupert Murdoch’s newspaper The Sun. The scandal was covered up, the bereaved families were ignored, and no one was held accountable. There could have been no more brutal proof that these people did not really count.

Hillsborough provided, however, the first real evidence that Burnham is a politician with both emotional intelligence and moral purpose. When, as secretary of state for culture, media, and sport, he represented the then Labour government at the twentieth-anniversary memorial in Liverpool’s home ground at Anfield in 2009, his speech was interrupted by chants demanding justice for the victims. Burnham had the wit to stop talking and listen. The next day he pushed at cabinet for the creation of an independent investigative panel and new inquests. The final report, issued in 2012, resulted, in 2016, in ninety-six verdicts of “unlawful killing.”

Burnham’s speech on the ruling in the Commons was a passionate denunciation of “a police force that has consistently put protecting itself over and above protecting people,” a judicial system “that gives the upper hand to those in authority, over and above ordinary people,” and print media that colluded with the police to create a “false version of events” that lingered for almost thirty years. The speech was so powerful that, against parliamentary protocol, it drew sustained applause and cheering.

There was a bitter irony, however. Burnham delivered his philippic two months before the Brexit referendum. He gave voice to a proper antielitism, characterizing the Hillsborough cover-up as a “collusion between elites.” But that righteous anger was almost immediately diverted into the false antielitism of Brexit. Just as Donald Trump was doing in the US that year, Britain’s reactionary right surfed the waves of resentment against distant political institutions, corrupt justice systems, and cynically compliant media organizations.

Perhaps in recognition of this reality, Burnham staged his own revolt against Westminster, resigning as an MP and successfully contesting the election for the mayoralty of Greater Manchester in 2017. He won almost two thirds of the vote—a feat he repeated in 2021 and 2024. His media image as “King of the North” was burnished by his effective advocacy for the region during the Covid-19 pandemic and his skillful redefinition of “Manchesterism.” In the nineteenth century the term signified a radical commitment to laissez-faire economics as well as social liberalism. Burnham made it stand for an activist regional administration in which public utilities were returned to collective ownership and businesses worked in close partnership with local government—a combination that gave Manchester a relative dynamism under his leadership, an exception to Britain’s economic inertia.

Advertisement

He also articulated an opposition to the whole established Westminster system, which he described as a centralized hierarchy that only grudgingly conceded to popular democracy without ever really embracing it:

Westminster remains an antiquated world into which degrees of democracy were introduced as the franchise was extended. But, fundamentally, it remains the same: a system built to concentrate power in the hands of the already-powerful and that much has not changed through the centuries. This over-concentration of political power in one place in too few hands is the main reason why Britain is one of the most politically centralised and economically unbalanced countries in the developed world…. It is also the underlying explanation for more widespread failure.

Burnham’s accession to power thus raises two big questions for progressive politics across the democratic world: Can the left give nostalgia a meaning that is not reactionary? And can democratic governments give up some of their power not to private oligarchies but to communities and citizens who feel increasingly powerless? Burnham’s ability to provide credible responses to those questions may depend on the answer to a third one: Can the United Kingdom hold together?

Two thirds of the way through Burnham’s first big speech as prime minister, given at the Labour Party conference on September 29, he stopped speaking. Much of the audience, thinking he had lost his train of thought, rose to encourage him. But the pause was for dramatic effect and to gather himself for a passage he would deliver with a catch in his voice and an air of barely suppressed emotion. This was the moment that would be excerpted for social media feeds and TV reports. In it he fused his own personal nostalgia for a progressive British past with assurance that Britain still has a future as a unified polity.

A fortnight earlier, Burnham’s father, Roy, had died from complications of Alzheimer’s disease. On the same day, the first ministers of the three devolved governments of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland held a summit in Cardiff. John Swinney of the Scottish National Party, Rhun ap Iorwerth of Plaid Cymru, and Michelle O’Neill of Sinn Féin signed a joint declaration that “Westminster’s time is coming to an end”—an awkward assertion for Burnham because it is also what he himself (albeit with different implications) believes. Swinney made the prediction personal by suggesting that Burnham will be the last prime minister of the UK.

It would be wrong to suggest that Burnham cynically used this conjunction of personal sorrow and political challenge as an escape hatch from the complexities of the UK’s national questions. He nonetheless achieved that to brilliant effect. He quoted Swinney’s prophecy of doom and then pivoted to paternal piety:

Whatever its flaws, this country gave my dad a good life…. The United Kingdom my dad represented is the one I believe in. A union of nations that gave trade unions and the cooperative movement to the world. The National Health Service. A country that stood up to fascism. A country of solidarity, not separation. That’s the Britain my dad represented. Britain is not perfect. It can be better and we will make it so. But it still stands for something worth saving, worth fighting for. And we will always be stronger facing a changing world together, rather than separating.

Oratorically, this is tremendously effective—it distills hundreds of years of socialist history into the figure of his dear dead dad. Roy Burnham, who worked as a telephone engineer for the British postal service and then for the privatized British Telecom, was born in May 1941, when Britain still controlled more than a quarter of the world, the trains still stopped at Kenyon Junction, the collieries and ironworks were working overtime, and Albert Dock was a vital base for the British Atlantic fleet. Burnham, moreover, projected his vision of a united Britain back a generation further. Near the start of his speech, he reminded the party faithful that the conference was taking place on what used to be Liverpool’s working waterfront, and he dug back into his Boys from the Blackstuff memory bank: “For me, life truly has come full circle because this is where my story began. My granddad drove a lorry along these docks for Tate & Lyle.”

There’s an awful lot of death wrapped up in this rhetoric—a dead father, a dead world of industrial might, the death foretold of the United Kingdom that Burnham was pledging to defy, the death of the fictional George in Boys from the Blackstuff that brought tears to his mother’s eyes because it reminded her in turn of her dead father. All these intimations of mortality are permeated with an air of nostalgic reverie, the “dreams of long ago” that give the dying George hope for the working class.

This backward glance is a more elegiac and plaintive version of the retrograde vision that animates ascendant right-wing movements: the “again” in MAGA, the “back” in the winning Brexit slogan “Take Back Control.” Burnham’s rhetorical question at the party conference was, “We led the world’s first Industrial Revolution from the Midlands and the North of England. So why can’t we lead the next?” The lost world can become a new world, one in which Britain (so long as it hangs together) can again be a global powerhouse.

Yet these stakes are far too high. If the future of the union is to be gambled on Britain regaining some equivalent of its world-shaping power in the nineteenth century, it seems a losing bet. The striking absence in Burnham’s evocation of the past is empire. This amnesia is convenient not just because it makes Britain’s “long ago” much more benign and progressive than it really was but because it evades the question of how a revived UK could lead the world without the raw might of conquest. The realistic aim now is surely to make Britain a successful member of what Canadian prime minister Mark Carney calls the “middle powers.” Delusions of grandeur merely get in the way of achieving it.

Burnham’s promise of resurrection also exposes the ambiguities within his own position as a leading figure in the centrifugal politics of the last two decades who nonetheless is now appealing for “solidarity not separation.” He evokes the first Industrial Revolution as a product specifically of “the Midlands and the North of England”—not London, not Wales, not Scotland, not Northern Ireland. This may be accurate enough, but it also draws on a particular regional story. Its emotional ground is the grief that lingers after the slow death of the North of England’s sense of itself as the engine room of world history.

Burnham is well aware that a large part of his mission is to confront the English question. The rise of English nationalism—itself driven in part by resentment at the devolution of powers to the three other nations—was at the heart of Brexit. Burnham wants to revisit that fateful decision and declares that “Brexit has done more harm than good.” He knows that he cannot get the economic growth necessary to implement a progressive agenda while Britain’s economy remains stymied by its perverse erection of barriers to trade with its most important market, the European Union. But even though Brexit was a phony response to the alienation of much of England, Burnham can’t just sweep it away. He has to replace it with a genuine response.

Hence one of Burnham’s signature moves—Number 10 North. He announced very quickly after he became prime minister that he will establish an equivalent of 10 Downing Street in Manchester and govern at least one day a week from there. He called Number 10 North the “nerve center of a rewired Britain” and promised that it will “oversee the biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen.” This might be surprising to those who live in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, who may wonder how it could be bigger than the establishment of elected parliaments and executives in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Belfast. The hidden assumption in Burnham’s phrase is that “our country” is England.

This is not to say that Burnham’s idea of “driving power out of Whitehall” and shifting it to the North of England is a bad one. It is merely to point out that there is a tension between his passionate support for the devolution of authority to more parts of the UK outside of London and his desire to shore up the union itself. The Westminster system that Burnham rightly sees as the culprit for Britain’s failures is highly centralized for a reason: it is hard to hold four nations together without a top-down culture of command and control. Dismantling that system while preserving the union is a risky business. Burnham shares with his nationalist opponents the desire to destroy Westminster—the difference being that he wants to destroy it in order to save the union, while they want to do so in order to kill it off.

Conservative unionists always believed that giving more autonomy to the smaller nations within the UK would not appease their sense of separateness but deepen it. In that, at least, they were right: the very existence of devolved parliaments validates a sense of national difference. Burnham, with his retreat from Westminster to Manchester in 2017, was declaring himself (though he would never put it this way) a North of England nationalist. Now that he occupies the dead center of the Westminster system, he has to both honor that impulse in himself and tame it in others.

There is a path through this maze. In 2022, when Labour was out of office, it established the Commission on the UK’s Future, chaired by Burnham’s former mentor Gordon Brown. Its report acknowledged the core British problem of

an unreformed, over-centralised way of governing that leaves millions of people complaining they are neglected, ignored, and invisible, all too often left to feel as if they are treated as second class citizens in their own country.

This unbalanced system had created a country in which “half the UK population live in areas no better off than the poorer parts of the former East Germany, poorer than parts of central and Eastern Europe…poorer than the US states of Mississippi and West Virginia.”

It recommended radical constitutional change: the abolition of the absurdly undemocratic House of Lords (made up of almost eight hundred unelected appointees); its replacement by an elected Assembly of the Nations and Regions; the devolution of economic power to all towns and cities in England and greatly enhanced self-government for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland; and an explicit constitutional commitment to ensuring the same standards of living across the UK.

Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, welcomed the report when he was in opposition but quietly shelved it as he approached the possibility of winning a general election. Giving away power is a very attractive idea until you have power yourself. One of the perennial problems of the British left has been its inability to resist the seductive idea that a system that exists, as Burnham has written, “to preserve the status quo” can be used to force through progressive change.

The starkest embodiment of this dilemma is the great majority of parliamentary seats Burnham has inherited from Starmer’s victory in the general election in 2024. Labour actually secured just one third of the vote, but the first-past-the-post electoral system gave it two thirds of the parliamentary seats, benefiting from a process designed to shore up central power by giving the winning party a commanding majority.

Burnham, however, has established a national commission on electoral reform, knowing full well that a fairer allocation of parliamentary seats would have given Labour a much-reduced majority—and in effect that some of his MPs would not now hold that title. Sweeping constitutional change along the lines of Brown’s recommendations would also reduce Burnham’s ability to dispense political patronage, not least his capacity to reward supporters with appointments to the House of Lords.

Implicit in Burnham’s drive to spread the UK’s wealth, moreover, is the reality that spending has to be directed away from London and its hinterland. The established test for large-scale infrastructural projects is that they provide the maximum possible return on investment. This means that money goes to those regions that are already most developed. As Burnham complained when he was mayor of Manchester, the official attitude is that “those old industrial communities can’t become anything again so why invest in them?” Turning this orthodoxy on its head and giving priority to the poorest places is not a direct attack on London, but its indirect consequences for the capital will become increasingly obvious.

In his pursuit of this radical agenda, Burnham’s enemy is time. Apart from everything else, Brexit has been a colossal waste of time. It distracted governments and civil servants and initiated the chronic political instability in which Burnham acceded to office as the seventh prime minister in ten years. He must now not only make up for lost time but accelerate profound changes to Britain’s constitution, its economic decision-making, and its industrial strategy, all while coping with chronic domestic and global crises.

Yet his advantage is that he has no choice but to be radical. More than any other British politician since Thatcher in 1979, he is defined by the sense of an ending. Thatcher believed that industrial Britain was moribund and proceeded to kill it off without pity or regret. Burnham believes that the postindustrial Britain she created is expiring in its turn and that, unless he can resurrect some version of the past she buried, it will take the UK with it. Rather than contenting himself with one last ride on that ghost train, he knows he has to lay down a whole new set of tracks.

entries.title: The Renters Take Providence
entries.summary: On September 9 the incumbent mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, Brett Smiley, lost his reelection bid to a twenty-seven-year-old democratic socialist named David Morales. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On September 9 the incumbent mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, Brett Smiley, lost his reelection bid to a twenty-seven-year-old democratic socialist named David Morales. It was the first time an incumbent mayor failed to win his party’s primary in the city’s history, and the latest in a wave of progressive victories over establishment Democrats that began with Zohran Mamdani last year.

Under the slogan “A Providence for All,” Morales emphasized the cost-of-living crisis, public education, protecting immigrants, and a Mr. Rogers-style neighborliness. He cut a whimsical figure on the campaign trail, in his signature bright blue suit and floral tie. In videos shot around the city, he shook hands with passersby as they recounted their struggles to pay rent, cover bus fare, and educate their children. The Smiley campaign spent more than $1.7 million, the lion’s share on television ad buys (much of it fear-mongering attacks on Morales for being soft on crime). The Morales campaign raised about $500,000, mobilized thousands of volunteers, and knocked 80,000 doors in a city of 190,000 people.

More than anything else, Morales ran on housing, which has become the animating issue in Rhode Island politics. When rents rose precipitously during the Covid-19 pandemic, Providence arguably felt the effects even more intensely than cities that had long been expensive, like San Francisco or nearby Boston. Between 2020 and 2024 the median rent increased more than 40 percent. In 2024 The Providence Journal reported that the city had seen the highest year-over-year rent increase in the country—16 percent. What was already a crisis for low-income Rhode Islanders became a problem for the middle class, too, as home values shot up all over town. More and more people entered homelessness for the first time.

The Providence left, including Morales, has spent the last six years arguing that the housing crisis epitomizes the inequality that defines our era. They have responded in part by organizing poor and working-class tenants to negotiate with their landlords for better conditions and more affordable rents. Smiley, meanwhile, sided with a political establishment that has catered to investors and wealthy transplants to Providence and blocked efforts to curtail landlords’ power over their tenants. In the eyes of many Rhode Islanders, he also came to represent the landlord class itself: although the Morales campaign almost never mentioned it on the campaign trail, it’s common knowledge in the state that Smiley owns three homes, including a modernist manse in the pricey beach community of Tiverton, and is married to the real estate tycoon Jim DeRentis.

This turned the mayoral race into a proxy for a broader contest between renters and the real estate industry over who would determine the city’s direction. The same themes were central to the campaigns of eight left-wing candidates for city council who ran alongside Morales—all of whom won their races, installing a progressive majority in City Hall. According to The Providence Journal, it was tenants who decided the election, with three renter-heavy neighborhoods likely delivering Morales’s victory.

A week after Morales won the primary, he celebrated his twenty-eighth birthday. He posted a photo on social media of a gathering at Charles Place, a subsidized housing development. Earlier in the summer, the tenants of that building formed a supermajority tenant union to demand that their landlord collectively bargain a new lease. In the photo, the presumptive mayor sat beaming in front of his cake, the members of the union—of his coalition—arrayed behind him.

Morales grew up in Soledad, California, where his mother raised him on her own. When we spoke after the primary, he remembered couch surfing when the family was between apartments, until they were able to secure a public housing unit when he was twelve years old. Diligent and driven from an early age, he graduated from the University of California, Irvine, as a teenager, and in 2019, at twenty, became the youngest person to complete Brown University’s public affairs master’s program.

The next year Morales challenged his state representative, Daniel McKiernan, who was running for a fourth term representing a working-class section of Providence. On the campaign trail he talked about housing, education, and the need to raise the minimum wage in Rhode Island, which at the time was $10.50 an hour, significantly lower than in neighboring states. Morales won, securing nearly 50 percent of the vote.

By the time he took office in 2021, everyone in Providence was talking about “the housing crisis.” There was a general sense that the moment’s defining issue had been met with an inept and inadequate response. Since 1991 all thirty-nine cities and towns in Rhode Island have been required to ensure that at least 10 percent of their housing stock meets affordability requirements, but as of last year only eight cities had reached the benchmark. Rhode Island ranks among the lowest in the nation for housing production. Activists covered the city in stickers reading “Freeze Rents, Not People,” the letters icy blue and snowcapped. More and more people stood on street corners and meridians with signs pleading for help.

Advertisement

For elected officials, the central question was what the government could or should do to address the problem. The state created its first-ever cabinet-level housing secretary position in 2022—a move that was intended to pave the way for a statewide housing plan, and which Morales supported—but in its first three years the department ran through as many directors. Meanwhile, establishment Democrats responded by trying to facilitate affordable housing production. Between 2022 and 2025, lawmakers in the state proposed historic bond measures alongside legislation that loosened regulations around accessory dwelling units, revised zoning laws and the state building code, and repurposed vacant buildings, among other measures. These policies promised more units and a more stable housing market in the future but didn’t ameliorate the struggle many Rhode Islanders faced writing their rent check every month. Of the fifty-two bills that leadership put forth in a four-year period, only one directly addressed tenant issues—a ban on rental application fees that had been introduced by one of Morales’s progressive colleagues in the statehouse, Cherie Cruz.

Smiley likewise responded in Providence by trying to spur developers to build housing. He eased zoning regulations, sped up permitting processes, and increased funding for new construction. In campaign literature this year, he claimed to have overseen the creation of thousands of new housing units across income levels during his term.* “I talked to people in the business community, construction and development people, along with nonprofit developers,” Smiley told me. “What we tried to do was do everything. It was our belief that there was no silver bullet.” In the most recent budget, Smiley also continued funding for legal services that provide eviction defense, as well as funding to enforce minimum housing standards, and proposed a $1 million fund that would provide up to $3,000 in emergency relief to people facing eviction or foreclosure. But although he acknowledged the crisis tenants were facing, he allocated far more resources to new development—through tax breaks and subsidies—than to tenant protections.

At the same time, a vision in which the public sector assumed more responsibility for the crisis was taking shape on Providence’s grassroots socialist left. One organization in particular, Reclaim Rhode Island, begun after Bernie Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, was increasingly focused on challenging the power of real estate developers, financial institutions, and landlords. Its first major foray into housing organizing was a 2022 campaign to create the country’s first state-level public developer. Modeled on efforts in Montgomery County, Maryland, and Seattle, Washington, such an institution would not only provide state-backed financing for building affordable housing, but also maintain public ownership—an alternative to the prevailing approach, which relies overwhelmingly on the private sector. The goal, Reclaim and its allies argue, is to build the kind of “social housing” constructed in Red Vienna in the 1930s: dense, thoughtfully designed apartment buildings that appeal to people at a range of income levels. Since 2022 the state has appropriated $20 million for public development, but the funds have ultimately been redirected to existing public housing authorities rather than put toward exploring a new model.

For Reclaim, the campaign went beyond the effort to build new units, as significant as that might be. “We are not ‘housing people’ who started a housing and tenant organization,” said Daniel Denvir, the group’s cofounder and current cochair (and the host of a popular left-wing podcast, The Dig). “We’re socialists who were exploring how to build power and decided upon housing as the way to do that.” To push the public developer model was to insist that the government should use public resources to reduce the power of the real estate industry and private financial institutions.

At the same time, Reclaim had started knocking on tenants’ doors. Nationwide, tenant organizing picked up steam during the Covid-19 pandemic; a few tenant union efforts had flared up in Providence but quickly fizzled out. Hoping to seed a broader movement of organized poor and working-class people, Reclaim pursued a strategy pioneered by the Connecticut Tenants Union and SEIU 1199 New England, in which tenants form a supermajority in a building and collectively bargain leases with their landlord.

The tenants of the first landlord Reclaim took on were living with floods, rodents, and malfunctioning toilets. Accustomed to being ignored, many were eager to talk to the organizers who showed up at their doors. “I was fighting all this on my own for the first, like, two years,” one woman—who had been trying in vain to get the landlord to fix her apartment’s exposed drywall, broken heaters, and cockroach infestation—told me when I reported on these efforts at the time. Within two years the group had helped organize the tenants of two corporate landlords who collectively owned more than four hundred units. But the project never coalesced into the statewide movement Reclaim envisioned. In both cases, the landlords retaliated, stoking fear among tenants, and novice organizers struggled to respond; the fledgling unions soon petered out. (They did result in legal action against the landlords; both cases are ongoing.)

Advertisement

Meanwhile, Morales had been working in the statehouse to advance tenant protection legislation. During his first two years in office, he introduced bills to limit rental application fees, cap rent increases, and replace lead pipes carrying water into people’s homes—but without a broad tenant movement behind them, and facing a well-funded landlord lobby, the bills never made it out of committee. (Morales did work on successful legislation that facilitated access to health care for pregnant people, lowered the price of insulin, and legalized cannabis, as well as a bill that required landlords to accept Section 8 housing vouchers, which preceded the leadership’s push to introduce housing packages.)

The attempts to empower tenants in their buildings and in the statehouse began to come together in late 2022. Reclaim was encountering an issue that often exemplifies landlord impunity in Rhode Island: childhood lead poisoning. Organizers met several families whose children had been exposed to lead paint, and at least one whose children were severely poisoned, despite state laws requiring landlords to safeguard tenants against such hazards. At around the same time, the attorney general in Rhode Island decided to prioritize enforcing lead laws and asked legislators to pass new protections. While Reclaim knocked doors, Morales and his progressive colleagues in the legislature (many of whom Reclaim and other left-wing organizations like the Rhode Island Working Families Party had helped to elect) introduced several bills to protect tenants from lead.

Reclaim and other housing advocacy groups backed the legislation and a bigger slate of pro-renter bills by turning out dozens of tenants to the statehouse for a rally. Morales spoke, as did Cruz (the two are among a small minority of lawmakers who are also renters). “We flooded the statehouse with over one hundred tenants in red shirts and delayed session from starting,” Morales remembered in a recent interview. “They made it very clear they had to pass tenant protections.”

In hearings over the next few months, fierce and coordinated opposition from landlords attempted to convey the opposite. One landlord wrote in a public comment that the rental registry law was “a gross, tyrannical step by the statewide government and an attack on a citizen’s privacy,” and “a blatant attack on those that are trying to provide housing.” Another threatened that he was “done in RI, because of your shenanigans, I am liquidating.” A third warned: “If you pass this, I’m going to evict every single tenant.”

Tenants also told their stories to lawmakers. One mom testified with a Ziploc bag of lead paint chips in her hand. Organizers from Reclaim had knocked on her door a few months earlier, and she was ready to speak out. “This is what falls off my walls every day, and this has lead,” she said at a hearing. “I have to live in fear of this right here falling off every day. And nothing gets done.” Less than two months later, the governor signed the lead safety measures into law.

Morales decided to primary Smiley in January 2025. At the beginning of the year, a polar vortex sent temperatures in Rhode Island into the teens. Homelessness outreach workers warned that many people faced spending the night outside, in tents. Since the pandemic, the state’s homelessness response system has been overwhelmed, leading to long waits for temporary shelter beds. Advocates called on Smiley to open an overnight emergency shelter for the duration of the cold snap, but he refused.

On the night of January 7, when the temperature outside was 17 degrees, two young, progressive city councilors, Miguel Sanchez and Justin Roias, decided to take action. Against the mayor’s orders, but with the blessing of the council president, they turned the city council chambers into a makeshift shelter for the night. At the time I covered housing in Rhode Island for the local NPR station. I showed up to find that they had worked with social service agencies to coordinate warm meals and a coat drive, and had placed a sign in front of the council chambers that read “Welcome, Warming Area / Bienvenido Área de calentamiento.”

Over the next few hours, dozens of people showed up to sleep on the benches in the council chamber. Many seemed tentative as they climbed up the marble stairs and passed through the heavy wooden doors. A team of legal observers stood by, and community members and other elected officials, including Morales, arrived to help. Donations of blankets, food, and hot chocolate poured in from the community. About thirty homeless people ultimately spent the night. So did Morales, who recalled in a recent interview that he left feeling an urgent need to respond further. “We had to keep our neighbors from dying on the street,” he said. “It made it very clear to me we needed a shift in leadership.”

At the time the Providence left was casting around for a way to build on its victories from 2023. Morales and other legislators, with the backing of Reclaim, spent two sessions pushing a package of legislation that they named a “tenant bill of rights.” At its core were just cause eviction protections, which prevent landlords from evicting tenants unless they have a qualifying reason. Two years in a row, the bills died in committee. “It was clear we’d hit a wall,” Denvir told me in a recent interview. “We had some power in the statehouse, and we had achieved everything we could with that power.”

But a new fight over housing was taking shape in the city council. The council president, Rachel Miller, had expressed support for the idea of a rent stabilization ordinance when she began her term in 2023, while Smiley, then the incoming mayor, had made clear that he opposed such a measure. In the summer of 2025 a special election for a city council seat in one of Providence’s toniest neighborhoods unexpectedly became a referendum on the issue; after an establishment candidate came out adamantly against rent stabilization, voters chose the only candidate who supported it (she also got a boost from a Reclaim endorsement and the organization’s help campaigning). In January Miller introduced the ordinance.

Rent stabilization became a new focal point for the debate about how the government should respond to the housing crisis. The proposal fiercely divided the city council, but a coalition of groups, including Reclaim, worked to secure a majority, and the measure passed in April. Polling showed 74 percent of likely Democratic voters in Providence supported it (only 59 percent of households rent in the city). Yet Smiley vetoed the law as promised. He said in our interview that he “did it on principle because it’s wrong for the city,” and that “sometimes you have to do what’s right, even if it’s unpopular.” That decision made David Morales the rent stabilization candidate. Morales’s campaign was already focused on the cost-of-living crisis, but after the veto he began to more explicitly cast the mayor as the pro-developer, anti-tenant choice. “That was the evidence that we needed to solidify to our neighbors that the city mayor is not on the side of working people,” Morales said. It showed, he told me, that “we had a mayor that was more susceptible to corporate interests than he was paying attention to the needs of our community.” 

The rent stabilization fight also fueled a number of other primary races in the city and the state—especially after the council failed by a single vote to overturn the mayor’s veto. To left-wing groups that had scrambled for a supermajority, the city councilor who decided their defeat was John Goncalves, who represents Ward 1, which encompasses much of the Brown University campus, all of downtown, and the mostly residential neighborhood of Fox Point. That neighborhood, which was once the heart of Rhode Island’s Cape Verdean community before a highway redevelopment project displaced many residents, has among the highest density of renters in the city, many of whom are college or graduate students. Campaign finance records show that Goncalves received large political donations from real estate developers and the landlord lobby in Rhode Island. The day of the vote, he sent a clear message when he neglected to show up in the council chambers.

In June Miguel Martinez Youngs, a policy staffer for the city council who was the principal author of the rent stabilization ordinance, quit his job to primary Goncalves. (Prior to working for the council, Youngs was first the organizing director and then a cochair of Reclaim.) Over the course of the campaign, Goncalves spent over $140,000 dollars—believed to be the most any city council candidate has ever spent on a race in Rhode Island. Youngs spent just over $20,000, and drew for his field operation on the coalition of progressive political organizations and volunteers that had also coalesced behind the Morales campaign. He ran on a clear message: he was the guy who wrote the ordinance, and he was challenging the guy who ensured it never became law.

In electing Youngs and his allies, many Providence residents seemed to be consciously voting for their own interests as renters. To Reclaim, this was a clear vindication of its strategy. After its first two tenant union campaigns dissolved into slow legal processes, the group raised money to hire full-time organizers, including a former union staffer from the militant SEIU 1199 New England who brought his experience with labor to housing. The group with which Morales celebrated his twenty-eighth birthday, the Charles Place Tenant Union, is one of four supermajority tenant unions that Reclaim has helped organize in the past year, all of which are in the process of collectively bargaining leases with their landlords; Reclaim envisions them as the first chapters in its project to build a statewide Rhode Island Tenants Union.

In the meantime, these unions may have tipped the scales in one of the fall’s closest city council races. Justin Roias, who had worked to turn the council chambers into a makeshift shelter that cold January night, and who has supported the tenant organizing efforts in his ward, faced a primary challenge from a pro-business centrist. On election day, the ward saw a 30 percent increase in voter turnout. Denvir of Reclaim suggested that formerly disaffected, now organized tenants may have been inspired to take part in the political process. Roias won by fifty-five votes.

At an election night party for the entire leftist slate on September 9, hundreds of people gathered in the courtyard of one of the repurposed mill buildings in Providence’s West End. The local brass band that often punctuates progressive gatherings in the city set the tone. Surrounded by the remnants of a long-gone industrial economy, campaign volunteers, local politicians, and the grassroots groups that carried Morales and his allies to victory gathered under a common vision for what the city could become. One after another, the candidates took the stage. Morales climbed the steps to chants of “David! David! David!” (Few people call him by his last name.) “Solidarity was on the ballot!” he proclaimed. “We chose to believe. We chose hope over fear.”

Also on the ballot: a movement that has swept leftists into city government in a growing number of places across the country—not just New York but Seattle, Ann Arbor, and Washington, D.C. As they take office, their challenge will be to deliver on a mandate for transformative change while facing down material constraints, especially fiscal ones. As Piper French wrote in a recent article about New York City DSA and the Mamdani administration in The Drift, “The terrifyingly high-stakes reward is the chance to make these intellectual questions material—to determine, together and apart, precisely what different could look like.”

The young Mamdani administration suggests just how complicated that task can be, as it tangles simultaneously with a federal government sending ICE agents into the city and a leftist base incensed by the NYPD’s collaboration with them—all while launching a 2-K program and filling more than 200,000 potholes. But unlike other socialist mayors, Morales will be working with a legislative branch that largely shares his vision for the city. A month after the primary, the Providence City Council threw its support behind the socialist Miguel Sanchez to serve as the next council president come January.

The Democratic establishment has yet to articulate a clear response to this wave of challengers. But the results in Providence show that a vague appeal to affordability falls short when twelve million tenant households in the United States spend more than 50 percent of their monthly income on housing. None of the candidates denied that the city and the state face a crisis. Yet as Morales’s campaign manager Ben Shanahan said in an interview, many establishment leaders still “refuse to actually commit to any material, immediate relief for people who really need it.”

Morales has vowed to sign a rent stabilization ordinance within his first one hundred days in office. He plans to establish a public developer at the municipal level, and to expand the city’s capacity to hold landlords accountable for unsafe living conditions. Smiley, meanwhile, has declined to endorse Morales in the general election. A few days after the primary, the outgoing mayor advertised a rental unit he owns at $5,500 a month—a 47 percent increase since 2020.

entries.title: ‘Natives of the Country’
